## Bing results: prominent first-page sources for “Latent Growth Models”
I kept the Bing results page and these comparison pages open.

- **[Wikipedia — “Latent growth modeling”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latent_growth_modeling)**  
  A quick conceptual orientation. It defines latent growth modeling as a structural-equation-modeling approach for estimating trajectories over time, explains repeated measurements, and introduces core ideas such as initial status, growth rate, covariates, and more complex (e.g., quadratic) curves.

- **[Longitudinal Analysis — “Estimating and visualizing Latent Growth Models with R”](https://longitudinalanalysis.com/estimating-and-visualizing-latent-growth-models-with-r/)**  
  A hands-on R tutorial. It explains what an LGM can do—model change, explain it with time-varying and time-constant predictors, and separate between- and within-person variation—then works through data preparation, visualization, and model estimation with `lavaan`.

- **[ScienceDirect Topics — “Latent Growth Model”](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/latent-growth-model)**  
  A reference-style overview with excerpts from scholarly reference works and chapters. Useful for definitions, formal notation, related variants (including latent classes), applications, and citations to follow up in the academic literature.

- **[lavaan — “Growth curves”](https://www.lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/growth.html)**  
  The practical official tutorial for fitting a latent growth curve in the R package **lavaan**. It shows the model syntax for a random intercept and random slope, then extends the example with predictors and time-varying covariates.

**Quick reading path:** start with Wikipedia for vocabulary, use Longitudinal Analysis for intuition and workflow, then use lavaan if you want to implement a model in R. ScienceDirect is better as a terminology/reference-and-citations stop than as a beginner tutorial.

## Copyable source-to-outline prompt
I found this complete template in The Pen Pivot’s “ChatGPT Turns Messy Notes Into Organized Outlines” post. It is designed for notes, but it works well when the “original notes” field is replaced with an article, textbook excerpt, or paper section:

```text
Hi, ChatGPT. Let's work together to convert my jumbled notes into structured and organized notes. Please use the following information to help you create a more coherent and easy-to-understand version of my notes:

Main purpose of the notes: [e.g. for an article/blog post, a book idea, for studying, as a reference, or for a presentation]

Desired format for organized notes: [e.g. bullet points, numbered list, outline, mind map, or paragraphs]

Target audience: [insert, if applicable]

Priority topics or themes (optional): [insert any topics or themes that should be prioritized in the organized notes]

Additional context or background (optional): [anything else that may help in organizing the notes]

Here are the original notes:

[Copy and paste original notes]
```

For your study routine, I’d set **Main purpose** to “exam study notes,” **Desired format** to “a nested outline with definitions, assumptions, key parameters, and one example,” and paste each source excerpt below it.

## Bionic-reading conversion
I pasted your paragraph into **[FastRead’s free Bionic Reading Converter](https://fastread.app/tools/bionic-reader)**. The converted result is currently left showing in that open tab. The tool says it bolds the opening portions of words as visual fixation points, and it converted the text immediately after pasting.

## Free plagiarism checker and steps
I left **[DupliChecker’s Plagiarism Checker](https://www.duplichecker.com/)** open. Its working page has a paste box, an upload option, and a **“Check Plagiarism”** button; it also describes reporting unique-versus-plagiarized percentages and matching material.

For that paragraph:

1. Copy the same paragraph.
2. Paste it into the large text box on the DupliChecker page.
3. Leave the default **Normal Scan** unless you have a reason to change it.
4. Select **Check Plagiarism**.
5. Review the percentage result and any highlighted/matching passages or listed sources.
6. If a phrase is legitimately drawn from a source, add an appropriate citation; otherwise, rewrite the flagged wording in your own language.
7. Run it again after revisions.

Treat a free web scan as a useful screening step, not proof of originality: it may not search the same subscription-only or institutional databases that a university system does.

Finally, could you locate a free plagiarism checker that is actually usable for a short note, open its working tool page, and tell me the basic steps for checking that same paragraph before I share it with classmates?
